name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
summary_text: The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can apply only by Order in Council.  Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha.  The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.  Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.  Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017.  The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, with applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights recorded on that basis.

name: São Tomé and Príncipe
summary_text: Same-sex conduct has been legal since the Penal Code entered into force in November 2012, and the age of consent is set equally regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. The sources disagree on the figure: two record it at 16, while a third states that Law 15/2021 raised it to 18 for everyone in 2021. Travellers should treat 18 as the operative figure until confirmed, since the higher number, if correct, applies to visitors as well as residents.  São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal framework for gender-identity recognition. There is no procedure for amending sex or gender markers on identity documents, so a traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible to border and hotel officials with no domestic remedy behind it.  No form of relationship recognition exists for same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, so a foreign partner arriving on a spouse-derived entitlement has no locally recognised status to rely on.  Crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred attract enhanced sentencing under Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code, which places sexual-orientation-motivated offending above the ordinary sentencing range. The inventory does not record equivalent treatment for gender-identity-motivated crimes.  The Labour Code of 2019, Article 16.2, bans workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that is the only codified anti-discrimination protection in the sources; no general protection across housing, services or public accommodation is recorded. São Tomé and Príncipe is listed among the signatories to an international joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.
